quiz.title: Module 1 — Tuesday — Understanding Audience & Purpose
quiz.description: Tuesday's quiz covers knowing your audience and knowing your purpose — why audience shapes how you communicate, why purpose shapes what you are trying to achieve, and what happens when either is missing.

questions.prompt: Why is it important for a writer to understand their audience before creating content?
options: It allows the writer to use more complicated vocabulary
It helps determine what information, language, and approach will be relevant
It guarantees that everyone will agree with the content
It allows the writer to avoid having a clear purpose
questions.explanation: Knowing the audience tells you what to include, what to explain, what language to use, and which angle will land.

questions.prompt: Which question helps a writer determine the audience's existing level of knowledge?
options: What platform should I publish on?
How long should my article be?
What does my audience already know?
What font should I use?
questions.explanation: Establishing what the audience already knows is how you find the right starting point.

questions.prompt: Why might the same idea need to be communicated differently to a beginner and an expert?
options: Experts prefer longer sentences
Beginners and experts have different levels of knowledge and therefore may require different approaches
Experts cannot understand simple explanations
Beginners should never be given detailed information
questions.explanation: Different levels of knowledge call for different approaches — the same idea, pitched differently.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a content purpose?
options: Increasing the number of words in an article
Making the writer sound intelligent
Educating the audience about a subject
Using as many writing techniques as possible
questions.explanation: Educating the audience is a purpose. Word count and technique are means, not ends.

questions.prompt: What can happen when content does not have a clear purpose?
options: The content may contain many words without actually accomplishing anything
The audience will automatically understand the message
The content becomes more persuasive
The writer becomes more creative
questions.explanation: Without a purpose you get plenty of words and no outcome — which is the trap the purpose questions are designed to prevent.

questions.prompt: Which set of questions best helps a writer clarify what they want their audience to experience or do?
options: What font should I use? What colour should I choose? What platform should I post on?
What do I want them to feel? What do I want them to think? What do I want them to do?
How many paragraphs should I write? How many words should I use? How quickly can I finish?
Who else is writing about this? How popular are they? How many followers do they have?
questions.explanation: Feel, think, do — the three questions that turn a purpose into something you can actually write toward.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between audience and purpose?
options: Audience determines what you want to achieve, while purpose determines who reads the content
Audience determines how you communicate, while purpose determines what you are trying to achieve
Audience and purpose are unrelated to the writing process
Purpose only matters after the content has been written
questions.explanation: Audience shapes how you say it; purpose shapes what the writing is for. Both decisions come before drafting.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, what should happen before a writer begins typing?
options: The writer should immediately start drafting
The writer should research competitors first
The writer should think about who they are writing for and why they are writing
The writer should choose a headline and publish it
questions.explanation: Good writing does not begin with typing — it begins with thinking about audience and purpose.
